Urban systems · GHSL and night lights · 2000 to 2025

Territorial Development Explorer

How is each city growing, and how close does it sit to the cities driving growth in its own country? The explorer answers both for 5,423 urban centres. Change the assumptions to fit a country's geography and data, and every map, count and description updates. New here? Read the guide with Morocco and Egypt examples.

STEP 1

Growth type

Each city's growth in night lights, population and built-up area is compared with the other cities of its own country. The dimension that leads sets the type: Leading, Pressure, Sprawl or Lagging.

STEP 2

Exposure to growth

Leading-Spillover Exposure adds up the economic mass of the country's Leading cities, discounted by distance. Two neighbours of a million people each, 50 km away, count the same under market access even if one grows 10% a year and the other shrinks 10%. Here only the growing one counts. Exposure is high when large growing cities are close; a small growing town next door adds little.

STEP 3

System-aware category

Crossing type with exposure splits Leading cities into Anchors and Isolated Poles, and Lagging cities into Connected Peripheries and Structurally Lagging places.

Focus

Pick a country to zoom in, read its profile and tune the settings to its geography. You can also click any city on the map.

Growth window

Five-year windows show recent shifts. A long window shows the structural pattern and is steadier. Types describe growth over the window, not a permanent label.

Exposure to growth
Distance decay

How fast a leading city's pull fades with distance. Low values spread exposure across the whole country; high values keep it local. The paper uses 1.5.

Distance at which a leading city's pull falls to about a third. Set it near the typical distance between cities in the country; the country profile suggests a value.

Only leading cities within this distance count, all equally. Read it as a commuting or market radius.

Mass of leading cities

Night lights understate activity where electrification is incomplete or much activity is informal. Population is cruder but steadier in those settings.

A city counts as highly exposed when its exposure is above this percentile within its own country. 50 is the median. Raise it to keep "connected" for the most exposed places.

Classification

Countries with fewer urban centres stay unclassified, because averages over a handful of cities are unstable.

Scroll or pinch to zoom · drag to pan · click a city to open its country

Reading the results

Labels are relative

Every test compares a city with its own country's average. A Leading city in a slow-growing country may grow less than a Lagging city elsewhere, and a city can lead while its lights dim if its compatriots dim more. Compare countries by their mix of categories, not by individual labels.

Types describe a window

Only about 40% of cities keep the same type from one five-year window to the next. Treat a type as a description of growth over the chosen period. The long-run window gives the steadier structural picture.

Night lights are a proxy

Lights track economic activity well on average but understate it where electrification is incomplete, settlement is sparse or activity is informal. In low-income systems, read Pressure shares as an upper bound and try population as the mass of leading cities.

Distance is straight-line

Exposure uses great-circle distance between city centres. Mountains, missing roads, sea crossings and borders all make real access worse than shown. Exposure to cities across a national border is not counted.

Exposure is not impact

A nearby growth pole can lift its neighbours or draw their workers and firms away. LSE measures how exposed a city is, not which of these happens. Connected Peripheries are where that question is worth asking.

The latest window spans COVID-19

The pandemic disrupted activity and night lights during 2020 to 2025. Some regional patterns in that window are stronger than in 2015 to 2020, so read it alongside earlier windows.

Data: GHSL Urban Centre Database R2024A (European Commission JRC) for urban centres, population and built-up area; harmonised DMSP-OLS/VIIRS night-time lights (Li et al. 2020); World Bank income groups and regions, with Afghanistan and Pakistan grouped under Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan (MENAAP); borders from Natural Earth. The 2025 lights value is the 2024 observation.

Method: Park, H. (2026). Measuring territorial development from publicly available data: a typology of cities and their exposure to growth. Manuscript under review. Paper settings: 2020 to 2025, gravity decay with α = 1.5, night-lights mass, median split, at least 5 cities per country.
